note: Where a browser client for a version can come from. An engine compiles (or reimplements) a Minecraft client for the web; this repository orchestrates them: it discovers versions, decides which engine can build one, and publishes what comes out. Adding an engine here is how a version family becomes buildable.

engines.name: CheerpJ + cheerpj-natives: the official client, unmodified
engines.note: No compile and no copy of the game: a real JVM (CheerpJ 4, Java 8/11/17) runs the official jar the visitor's browser downloads from Mojang, with the platform layer provided as JS natives (cheerpj-natives implements LWJGL). Textures, UI and behaviour are Mojang's because the jar is Mojang's and untouched. Coverage is the LWJGL 2 era: everything up to 1.12.2. Versions from 1.13 on use LWJGL 3, whose JS native layer does not exist yet - that single gap is what keeps 1.13 to 1.20.4 out, and Java 21 keeps 1.20.5 and later out of any JVM-in-page route. Classic versions fit here too: Indev, Alpha and Beta used LWJGL 2 and kept their textures inside the jar, which is exactly the case this route is good at.
engines.mods: runtime - real .jar mods for these versions load with no rebuild, because this is a real JVM

steps: resolve the official client jar url for the version (tools/update.py does this from Mojang's manifest)
the page fetches that jar in the visitor's browser - never from this site
cheerpjInit with javaProperties java.library.path pointing at the JS natives
cheerpjRunMain('net.minecraft.client.Minecraft', classpath of lwjgl + the client jar)

engines.caveat: LWJGL in JavaScript is described by its authors as partial. Browsercraft proves 1.2.5 and WebForge proves 1.6.4 with Forge; the Alpha/Beta/Indev ones use the same runtime path and older assets, so treat them as 'should work, test before advertising'.
engines.how: Nothing is compiled and nothing is copied: the visitor's browser fetches the official jar from piston-data.mojang.com, CheerpJ runs it with the JS natives on java.library.path, and the main class is net.minecraft.client.Minecraft. Our site serves only code: CheerpJ's loader, cheerpj-natives (Apache-2.0) and the LWJGL jars (BSD).

engines.name: Eaglercraft 26.2 workspace (TeaVM + WASM-GC toolchain)
engines.note: The Eaglercraft lineage for 26.x: the official client's source, patched with the browser platform layer, plus a real build system (Gradle for the Java, node scripts in wasm-toolchain/ for the link and the single-file package). Mods are compiled in through source hooks, so a mod set is a build.
engines.mods: yes - source hooks (see ../webmc-browser/modded/loader.py, which plans and prunes a Fabric mod set before the build)
notes: The repository is the already-patched project, so the CLI steps above are the whole build. Starting from the author's patcher kit instead means the patcher does the extraction once (Java 17), then the same commands build it.
Builds want ~10 GiB of heap and about forty minutes on a capable machine; the workspace ships run-memory-capped.js for machines with less.
Audio needs FFmpeg 6.1.1 only if you rebuild the sound archives; a normal build does not.
engines.blocked_by: no licence: the repository has no licence file, which means all rights reserved rather than free to use. Its 26.2 build was replaced by the MIT-licensed gaius engine, which covers 1.21.11, 26.2 and 26.3. Its compiler also reads sounds.epk unconditionally, which is why tools/empty-epk.init.gradle.kts exists: a build from this lineage has to create an empty archive with the engine's own packager (and give the optional music-pack export a name it accepts) rather than ship Minecraft audio.
engines.license_note: no licence file: all rights reserved rather than free to use. Its 26.2 build was replaced by the MIT-licensed gaius engine; re-enabling it is a licence decision, and CREDITS.md records it.

engines.name: EaglercraftX (the original 1.8 lineage)
engines.note: Where the Eaglercraft platform layer comes from: 1.5.2, 1.8.8 and 1.12.2, each a patched source tree compiled with TeaVM. Its layout (game/, platform-teavm/, a link step, a single-HTML package) is what the modern workspaces inherited, so the same build steps apply. Its TeaVM builds are the ones with tuned performance on the web; prefer them over the CheerpJ route when smoothness matters more than unmodified fidelity.
engines.mods: JavaScript only - these builds carry the EaglerForge-style mod API, not a JVM
notes: The release assets are the clients, and older mirrors of them are what the community plays; the repository itself is the engine.
engines.license_note: no licence file in lax1dude/eaglercraftx: all rights reserved. Not built from here; kept as the lineage reference for the workspaces, and credited in CREDITS.md.

engines.name: EaglerPorts (TeaVM ports of classic versions)
engines.note: One repository per old version, each publishing its own offline WASM build. No compile step here: the release asset is the client.
engines.license_note: EaglerPorts repositories carry no licence file: all rights reserved. This engine only *links* other people's builds where they live; nothing is copied or rebuilt from it.

engines.name: WebForge (CheerpJ: a real JVM, real jars)
engines.note: A JVM in the page, so Forge jars load at runtime with no rebuild. Old versions only (its class library is Java 8 era), but it is the one place where a .jar loads in a browser.
engines.mods: yes - real .jar files, loaded at runtime
engines.license_note: no licence file in Cucuzacu/WebForge: all rights reserved. A real-JVM route (Forge 1.6.4 under CheerpJ) that is linked, not rebuilt, until its licence is settled.

engines.name: Gaius (TeaVM, official client bytecode)
engines.disabled_why: Kept only as a record: it compiles the official client for 1.21.11/26.2/26.3 with a fully headless CLI, but each version needs its own hand-written profile, and its support stops at the versions it ships. Disabled by request; the Eaglercraft workspaces above are the preferred engines.
engines.mods: yes - build-time, through this repository's own bake (tools/bake_mods.py): the mod's classes are copied into the client and its entrypoint is called from the client's own initialiser. Mixins are the next step and the report says which mods have them.

profile_rules.why: the whole 1.21 line shares one client generation; a profile for 1.21.11 already exists and the profile for any other 1.21.x is generated from Mojang's own metadata
profile_rules.caveat: a version between the known ones starts from the nearest profile's overrides and its bring-up list, and the log says which patches were skipped

profile_rules.why: the engine ships a hand-written profile for 1.21.11 only, and its own tooling generates one for the 26.x line from Mojang's metadata - the versions it documents as supported (26.2 and 26.3). The generated profile starts from the nearest known profile's overrides and bring-up list, and the build log says which patches were skipped rather than pretending they ran.
profile_rules.caveat: a version whose patch chain has moved on since the profile was written fails on a version-specific patcher and needs one line in tools/aot_fixups.json - that is what the fixups file is for, and why the log records each skip.

engines.note: Enabled for the 26.x range: tools/aot_snapshot.py generates the profile from Mojang's metadata, so a new snapshot is a dispatch rather than a code change. The 26.1 - 26.3 range is generatable; 26.4 and later need the renderpearl renderer ported first, which is recorded as a blocker rather than promised as a build. In this project's v1 scope it builds 1.21.11 and, through generated profiles, the rest of the 1.21 line. 26.x is deliberately out of scope.

blockers.blocked_by: 26.4-snapshot-4 replaced the render layer: com/mojang/blaze3d/pipeline/RenderPipeline and ShaderSource are gone in favour of com/mojang/renderpearl/api/pipeline/*, and VertexFormat moved. The engine's symbol prober refuses a jar that has both, which is what its 26.3 patch chain produces on a 26.4 client (build run 38549140842: 'ModernSymbols: inconsistent client jar ... 26.2 render class ... is still present next to renderpearl').
blockers.work: a browser patcher for the renderpearl renderer. This is engine work, not a profile: everything the generated profile can supply - java level, protocol, pack versions, sha1s, overrides, bring-up entries - was already supplied before that error.

engines.audio: the client fetches its audio at play time; nothing in this repository ships Minecraft sound or music

engines.mods: runtime - a real class loader, so Fabric Loader and its mixins are the ordinary ones. Unproven: the same Fabric boot that is reported to hang under CheerpJ has to be re-tried on this runtime, which is a different class-loading implementation.
blockers: LWJGL 3's natives have to be compiled into the wasm module (GLFW 3, GLES3 over WebGL 2 and OpenAL all exist in emscripten; what is missing is the JNI layer that maps LWJGL's expected symbols onto them). tools/lwjgl3_surface.py already measures exactly which symbols that is.
the JDK 21 recipe needs porting to JDK 25 for the 26.x clients (Zero itself builds fine there)
performance is unknown: Zero is an interpreter, so this is the route for correctness and mods, not for frames per second - the compiled rows stay ahead of it on speed
engines.note: Kept disabled on purpose: it has no built client and a plan that offered it as playable would be lying. The route, the recipe and the link kit are real, and MODERN-JAVA.md is the account of what each remaining piece is.

rules.release: A release is a real client: buildable by an engine with a matching profile, otherwise it needs a workspace for that version.
rules.snapshot: Snapshots move weekly and can change the platform layer a workspace patches. They are catalogued and queued rather than built blindly.
rules.old_beta: Old versions have a different asset layout; use a classic engine.
rules.launch: Runs the official client unmodified in a JVM inside the page: nothing is compiled and nothing is copied, the visitor's browser fetches the game from Mojang. This is the only verdict where the textures and UI are guaranteed to be exactly Mojang's, because the jar is Mojang's.

references.name: Browsercraft (the CheerpJ team's own demo)
references.note: Minecraft 1.2.5 with the original JAR used untouched: the page fetches the client from piston-data.mojang.com in the visitor's browser. This is the pattern the launch route follows, and the cleanest UI to copy.

roadmap.blocked_by: LWJGL 3 has no JavaScript native layer (LWJGL 2 has one; Java is fine, CheerpJ runs Java 8 and 17)
roadmap.work: implement LWJGL 3's native methods in JavaScript. Measured on LWJGL 3 itself: the GL core classes Minecraft uses (GL11C, GL15C, GL20C, GL30C, GL32C) declare one native per entry point, about 270 in total, each a thin mapping onto a WebGL 2 call; GLFW is dispatched by function address (apiGetFunctionAddress + JNI.call*), so it needs a dozen dispatcher natives plus a name-to-JavaScript table for roughly 120 window/input functions; OpenAL is about 70 natives; STB about 15. tools/lwjgl_surface.py measures the subset a given client actually uses, which is smaller than the declared total.
roadmap.unlocks: unmodified official clients from 1.13 to 1.20.4, with real .jar mods and Mojang's own textures
roadmap.effort: bounded and mechanical: WebForge already did the equivalent for LWJGL 2 in about 2,200 lines of JavaScript, and this is the same kind of work for a larger API
roadmap.why_not_install: the LWJGL 3 jars are not the problem - they come from Maven like any library. The natives are: on a desktop they are .dll/.so/.dylib files that talk to the OS GL driver, and in a browser the only thing that can answer a native method is JavaScript.
roadmap.alternative: versions in this range can also be served ahead-of-time by a TeaVM workspace, which needs no JS natives at all because the platform layer is Java. That trades runtime mod loading for per-version build work.
alternatives: ahead-of-time: a TeaVM workspace for the version, no JS natives needed, mods baked in
CheerpX/WebVM: a real Linux in the page running a real JDK with Mesa, so the real LWJGL .so files work and no JS layer is written - 32-bit only and slow, but it removes this whole project

roadmap.blocked_by: CheerpJ supports Java 8, 11 and 17; 1.20.5 and later need Java 21, and 26.x needs Java 25. CheerpX cannot cover it either: it runs 32-bit x86 only, and Java 21 onwards ships 64-bit only.
roadmap.work: nothing we can do from here: it needs the runtime to ship a newer Java. Until then these versions go the ahead-of-time route (the Eaglercraft workspaces) or get streamed from a machine of ours
roadmap.unlocks: a real JVM for the newest versions
alternatives: ahead-of-time: a TeaVM workspace compiles the official client for the version (this is how 26.x is done everywhere, including by the Eaglercraft family)
streamed: a real JVM on a machine of ours, shown in a browser tab - real Java, but hours of a computer somebody owns

runtimes.name: CheerpX / WebVM (Leaning Technologies)
runtimes.java: whatever the guest installs, within its architecture limit
runtimes.license: proprietary, free for personal and open-source use

runtimes.name: TeaVM workspaces (the Eaglercraft lineage)
runtimes.java: any - the game's bytecode is a compile target, not something to execute
runtimes.gives: the newest versions, which no JVM in a page can run; mods compiled in at build time
limits: no runtime mod loading (no class loader in an ahead-of-time client)

runtimes.name: OpenJDK (Zero) compiled to WebAssembly - emscripten-forge
runtimes.license: GPL-2.0 with the Classpath exception (the JDK), Apache-2.0 (the kit)
runtimes.gives: a real JVM with a real class loader, in a page: System.loadLibrary, JNI, reflection and Fabric's class transformation are the ordinary ones, not a reimplementation. Threads are real (pthreads + SharedArrayBuffer), AWT/Swing run on x11.wasm, and the whole thing is statically linked into one wasm module that a static host can serve in chunks.
limits: Zero interpreter only: there is no JIT for wasm32 in this port, so a game can be correct and slow
no dynamic loader: every native method is answered from an emscripten_static_symbols table built at link time, so a native library must be compiled into the module
the recipe builds JDK 21; JDK 25 is the same port with a version bump, unproven here
posix_spawn does not exist, so anything that shells out has to be stubbed
runtimes.note: This is the only route found that runs Java 21+ bytecode in a browser at all. It is what the aot row is not: a class loader at play time, which is what Fabric needs.

builds_note: builds.json lists every browser build this project catalogs (GitHub only), and tools/fetch_builds.py downloads them into work/builds/ with a size and a sha256 each. Versions with no verifiable GitHub build are absent on purpose: 1.18.2 (the only repository is empty) and 1.21.5 / 1.21.11 (no single-file client published on GitHub that could be checked).
